]. Introduction

This style manual is intended primarily for use by WHO editors
working in English. Its main purpose is to ensure that the language used
in WHO publications is clear and correct and that the scientific and
other special nomenclature and terminology, abbreviations and sym-
bols are reasonably consistent and follow established international
precedents.

Editors should treat the manual as a work of reference to be consulted
in case of doubt, and not asa standard against which all details of every
manuscript must routinely be matched. Time should not be spent in
the pursuit of unif

2. Spelling

This section is a general guide to spelling used in WHO publications,
and also gives guidelines on hyphenation and capitalization. It is not
intended to be comprehensive, but to cover the main areas, such as
scientific and medical terminology, and names of places and organiza-
tions, where confusion and uncertainty may arise.

Within WHO, British rather than American spelling is normally used.
The general rule is to follow the first spelling listed in the latest edition
of The concise Oxford dictionary. If a variant spelling is listed separately,
the one to which you are referred

blocks.title: Page 9

WHO Editorial Style Manual

Eponymous names give no information about the nature of the disease
and different names may be used in different countries. They should be
avoided whenever possible. The Saxon genitive (’s) is not necessary
when using an eponymous name; e.g. Crohn disease, not Crohn’s
disease, and Down syndrome, not Down’s syndrome.

For general reference, Butterworths medical dictionary, 2nd ed. (Critchley
M, ed. London, Butterworths, 1978) and Dorland’s illustrated medical
dictionary, 28th ed. (Philadelphia, Saunders, 1994) can be recom-
mended for British and American spelling, r

Hyphenation

Hyphensare used to connect words that are more closely linked to each
other than to the surrounding syntax. Unfortunately there are no hard
and fast rules about their use. Certain conventions exist, but if there is
a choice it is better to introduce hyphens only to avoid ambiguity.
There is an overall tendency to use hyphens less than in the past and
a few general rules are applicable, as follows.

Hyphen after a prefix

A hyphen should be used after a prefix in order to prevent the word
being mistaken for another one, e.g. co-op, coop (but cooperate needs
no hyphen); re-cover, re

Capitalization

Too many capital letters break the flow of the eye across a sentence and
down acolumn of type. However, proper names, titles and institutions
require capitals. Descriptive appellations, such as administrative posts,
do not, unless the result would appear odd or confusing.

The trade names of drugs and other proprietary products, e.g. Pyrex and
Vaseline (petroleum jelly preferred), require an initial capital letter.
Generic terms in the Linnaean classification also take an initial capital
letter, e.g. Staphylococcus aureus, Trypanosoma, Schistosoma, b

3. Punctuation

This is a large subject where personal taste and common sense are more
important than any rules. Appropriate punctuation will ease reading
and clarify meaning, and this should be its purpose.

A well written running text should require only the minimum of
punctuation in order to read clearly and sensibly. If much punctuation
is required, it is probably a good indication that the texthas been badly
written and should be revised rather than heavily punctuated. Particu-
larly in scientific writing, unnecessary punctuation should be avoided
if the meaning is clear.

The punctuation

Comma

Correct usage of the comma is often a question of judgement. Commas
are now used much less frequently than in the past, and their main
purpose is to indicate a pause or to avoid ambiguity.

In a list of three or more items, a comma should in general be
consistently inserted or omitted before the final “and”, e.g.

X, Y and Z or X, Y, and Z.

Editors should ensure that each publication is internally consistent in
this respect. However, even when the “X, Y and Z” system is ado

3. To indicate that the second statement is an explanation or

Parenthesis

A parenthesis can be marked off by commas, dashes or brackets,
depending upon the closeness of its relationship to the sentence.

Parentheses should be used sparingly since they tend to break up
sentence structure and can too often be used to save the trouble of
organizing one’s thoughts.

5. Footnotes

Footnotes are used to give explanatory or supplementary details when
insertion in the text itself is not advisable, because the insertion would
break the continuity of the text unduly, because of the length of the
passage, or because the details were added by someone other than the
author. Such details might include references, explanations of unfa-
miliar terms, last-minute additions or editor’s notes.

The number of footnotes should be kept to a minimum. As a general
tule, veryshort notes, suchas cross-references to other sections or pages
of the same article or work, should be

blocks.title: Page 25
blocks.content:
WHO Editorial Style Manval

Ifa footnote refers to a quotation, the reference mark should be placed
after the final quotation marks.

Editor’s notes

Notes supplied by an editor, translator or compiler in a work including
original notes by the author must be differentiated from the original
notes. Such notes may be numbered in sequence with the author’s
notes.

Paragraphing and style

The paragraphing of footnotes should be in keeping with the overall
design of the book.. They may be set flush or in regular indented
paragraph style. Each footnote should end with a full stop.

6. Quotations

All quotations from printed material should correspond exactly to the
original in wording, spelling, punctuation, use of capital letters, etc.
When part of the original text is omitted from a quotation, the passage
in question should be replaced by three spaced dots. When three points
are used at the end of an incomplete sentence a fourth full point should
not be added. However, where the sentence is complete, the closing
point is set close up, followed by three points for omission. Omissions
should not change the meaning of the quotation.

7. Transliteration

It is usual to transliterate Arabic and Russian from their original
alphabets to the Latin alphabet, and to transcribe Chinese into Latin
characters, ie. to romanize the language. Editors should consult the
Office of Language Services (TRA) if they are in any doubt about the
transliteration of particular words or phrases.

Chinese

The romanization system called pinyin, introduced by the Chinese in

Pinyin should be used in all WHO publications; accents are not
generally necessary, except in certain specific contexts (e.g. texts on
acupuncture). Pinyin spellings often differ markedly from the older

9. Reference lists and bibliographies

A clear distinction should be made between lists of references and
bibliographies. A list of references contains only those works cited in
the text as sources of data or other information. It may include
unpublished documents, provided that these are available to inter-
ested readers. A bibliography is a list of published works relevant to
the subject matter of the publication and recommended for further
reading.

Authors are responsible for ensuring the accuracy of bibliographic
information. However, the editor should check any details that are
obviously

12. Numbers, dates, time and units
of measurement

Numbers

In general, words should be used for the numbers one to nine and at the
beginning of sentences, and figures for 10 and above; however, editors
should use their judgement in individual cases. Figures should never-
theless always be used in specific numerical contexts (e.g. “day 3” or “a
factor of 2”). Numbers that constitute a series or range should usually
be written as figures if at least one of them is greater than nine, for
example “we treated 19 patients with drug A and 7 with drug B”.

When anumber has more than four digits, it s

plural, and are not followed by a full stop unless they occur at the end
of a sentence.

Figures should always be used with unit symbols and abbreviations, for
example 7 kg not seven kg; the figure should be separated from the unit
symbol by a thin space. To avoid ambiguity, no more than one solidus
should be used to divide units, for example m/s? (or m-s~?) not m/s/s.
When a medial multiplication point is used, it should be clearly
identified.

Exceptionally, for blood pressure, values may still be given in millimetres
of mercury with the equivalent in kilopascals

15. Non-discriminatory language

Of the examples of discrimination that are most likely to be encoun-
tered in manuscripts, the most common involve discrimination on the
grounds of sex. For this reason, the guidelines presented here concen-
trate largely on means of avoiding overt or implied sex discrimination.
However, examples of racial or cultural discrimination may also be
found, and many of the principles that apply to the elimination of
sex discrimination can also be applied to the eradication of other types

of bias.

Modifying the way people speak and write is not easy, and there is —

blocks.title: Page 69
blocks.content:
WHO Editorial Style Manual

Non-sexist language — a cumbersome solution?

With care, the results of rewriting text to eliminate discriminatory
language will be no less concise than the original — but will be unam-
biguous and will avoid causing offence. For example:

“He may see himself as the pivot of all that happens. Hallucinations,
especially of hearing, are common and may comment on the patient
or address him.”

There will be occasions when a term including “man” may be unavoid-

example is “man-made disasters”, for which no generally acceptable
alternative is available. Use of the word “Chairman” rather than the
more general “Chair” or “Chairperson” may be obligatory. It would be
wrong to be over-dogmatic in this area: editors should exercise their
judgement, based on the principles outlined here.

16. Politically and legally sensitive topics

Occasionally, manuscripts contain statements that may cause offence
tocertain Member States, or references to geographical entities whose
name or ownership is disputed. It would be unrealistic to try to provide
a comprehensive list of sensitive topics, and editors need to be alert to
potentially controversial issues. These may include, for example,
terminology that implies a Euro-centric view of the world (Middle
East, Far East), references to countries as underdeveloped, and sugges-
tions that a particular government is corrupt. As a general rule,

to cover such cases.

If anything is to be said about the status of non-self-governing terri-
tories, they should be referred to as “territories that are not responsible
for the conduct of their international relations”; the words “colony”
and “colonial” should not be used.

Manuscripts submitted for publication in the Technical Report Series
